title: The Demographic Transition and Its Built-In Momentum
text:
Let me set out a model demographers use to describe how populations change as societies industrialise. It is called the demographic transition, and it is usually presented in four stages.

In the first, birth rates and death rates are both high and roughly cancel each other out, so the population grows slowly and is repeatedly set back by famine and epidemic disease. In the second, death rates fall, through better nutrition, clean water, sanitation and later medicine, while birth rates stay high. That gap between the two is what produces rapid population growth. In the third stage, birth rates fall as well, as more children survive, as families move off the land, and as schooling and paid employment for women expand. In the fourth, both rates are low and growth is slow once more. Two points deserve emphasis. The growth in stage two is not caused by people having more children; it is caused by more of their children living. And the process has momentum. A population containing many young people continues growing for decades after fertility has reached replacement level, simply because so many are still entering childbearing age. The model describes a pattern rather than a law, and societies have moved through it at very different speeds.
points: The demographic transition describes population change as societies industrialise, in four stages.
In stage one, high birth and death rates cancel out and population grows slowly.
In stage two, death rates fall through nutrition, clean water, sanitation and medicine while birth rates stay high, producing rapid growth.
In stage three, birth rates fall as child survival, urban life and women's education and employment change family decisions, and in stage four both rates are low.
Stage two growth comes from more children surviving, not from people having more children.
Population momentum means growth continues for decades after fertility reaches replacement level, and the model is a pattern, not a law.
